links.note: 951 says integrity and shame together are found 'naturally' (இயல்பாக) only in those born to a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண் அல்லது இல்லை). 972 says birth is alike for all living beings (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்) and that distinction differs only by what people do (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). The conflict holds if 972's பிறப்பு is taken to deny any inborn difference of character; Parimelazhagar softens it by reading 972 as the common nature of birth, leaving room for family.

951 claims that uprightness and shame (செப்பமும் நாணும்) come naturally to the well-born. 502 turns the same pair of ideas into a hiring test: trust goes to one who is குடிப்பிறந்து, free of fault, and has the shame that shrinks from a blemish (வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான்). The chapter on lineage states a belief; the chapter on choosing officers applies it, but adds freedom from fault as a separate check, so birth alone is not treated as enough.

952 says the well-born do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct, truthfulness and shame. 133 says having conduct is itself குடிமை and that a lapse (இழுக்கம்) turns into low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Read together, 952's claim is close to a definition: whoever slips has by 133 already left the class of the well-born, a point Parimelazhagar makes on 133 while keeping it within varna.

952 lists three things the well-born keep: ஒழுக்கம், வாய்மை, நாண். 983 lists five pillars that hold up சால்பு: love, shame (நாண்), obligingness, kindly regard and truthfulness (வாய்மை). Two of the three marks of lineage reappear as supports of personal worth, so the same core is described once as inherited and once as a structure a person stands on.

953 names a smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning (நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை) as the share of a true lineage. 92 takes three of these and ranks them: being sweet-spoken with a glad face (முகனமர்ந்து இன்சொலன்) is better than giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்). The list in 953 is flat; 92 shows the book elsewhere weighing its items against one another.

953 puts giving and not scorning (ஈகை ... இகழாமை) side by side among the marks of a good family; Parimelazhagar takes all four as the way one meets the poor who come. 1057 gives the receiver's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt (இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவார்), the asker's heart rejoices within. The pairing shows why 'not scorning' sits next to 'giving' in the list.

954 says the well-born will not do diminishing things (குன்றுவ) even if they get crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும்). 311 says the stainless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்). Both use the same 'even if they gained' (பெறினும்) form to set a fixed refusal against a large reward, once for family standing and once for non-harm.

954 says the well-born do not do things that diminish (குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர்), whatever the gain. 965 uses the same word to say what follows if they do: even those like a hill sink (குன்றுவர்) if they do a diminishing thing (குன்றுவ) the size of a kundri seed. 954 gives the rule and 965 the cost of breaking it, at a scale far below crores.

954 says no amount of wealth makes the well-born do what lowers them. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) ranks above gain reached by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). Both rank standing above wealth; 657 states the comparison outright, in the context of a minister's clean action.

955 says an old family does not part from its character (பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று) even when what it has to give has shrunk (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்). 223 says that giving without uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை ஈதல்) is found only in one who has lineage (குலனுடையான் கண்ணே). The chapter on giving and the chapter on lineage make the same claim from two directions.

955 says an old family keeps its character when its means of giving fall away. 218 says those who see what is due (கடனறி காட்சியவர்) do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). The same constancy under shrinking resources is credited to lineage in one verse and to understanding of duty in the other.

955 says an ancient family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its character when its means shrink. 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's speech (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்). They conflict if 1043 is read as plain poverty undoing lineage; the conflict eases on Parimelazhagar's reading, which stresses that 1043 calls poverty a craving (நசை), so it is the wanting, not the lack, that ruins.

956 says those resolved to live by their spotless lineage will not do unworthy things by taking to deceit (சலம் பற்றி). 660 uses the same word for wealth-making: securing wealth made by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள் செய்து) is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. 956 rules deceit out on grounds of family honour; 660 adds that its gains do not hold anyway.

956 says those who mean to keep to a spotless line do not do what lacks worth (சால்பில செய்யார்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even in poverty'. 656 says one should not do what the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை) even if one must see one's mother hungry. Both set a standard of worthy conduct above need, 656 naming the hardest case.

957 says a fault in the well-born shows up raised high, like the mark on the moon in the sky (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 433 says those ashamed of blame take a fault the size of a millet seed as the size of a palmyra (தினைத்துணை ... பனைத்துணை). 957 describes how the world sees a small fault in a prominent person; 433 describes the same enlargement done inwardly by the person, before the world does it.

957 uses the mark on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறு) as a figure for a fault that everyone sees because of where it sits. In 1117 the lover asks whether his beloved's face has a mark (மறு உண்டோ) as the bright full moon has. This is a lover's praise, not teaching, but both verses rely on the same fact: the moon's brightness is what makes its blemish known.

958 says that if lack of affection (நாரின்மை) shows in a man, people will doubt his lineage (குலத்தின்கண் ஐயப்படும்). 992 names having love and being born in a seasoned family (அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) as the two things that make up courtesy. 992 pairs love and birth as partners; 958 shows that when the first is missing the second is no longer believed.

959 says speech shows a person's lineage as a sprout shows the ground (குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல் காட்டும்). 1044 says that even in those of good birth (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும்) poverty brings the slackness from which degrading words are born (இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு). So the sign 959 relies on can be distorted by want: low words do not always mean low birth.

959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால் காட்டும்), and speech shows the family. 452 says water changes with the nature of the ground (நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்தற்று), and a person's understanding takes the nature of their company. Both use soil as the hidden source that marks what comes out of it, but one source is birth and the other is chosen company, which gives two different accounts of where character comes from.

959 treats the words from a person's mouth (வாய்ச்சொல்) as evidence of lineage. 139 says that for those who have conduct, speaking evil with the mouth is not possible even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்). Both make speech a reliable outward sign of something settled within, lineage in one and conduct in the other.

960 pairs நலம் with shame and குலம் with humility: want நலம், then want நாணுடைமை; want குலம், then want பணிவு toward all. 1019 uses the same pair in negative form: a lapse in principle burns one's குலம், and settled shamelessness burns one's நலம் (நலஞ்சுடும் நாணின்மை). The two verses share the குலம்/நலம் pairing and agree that நலம் depends on shame.

960 says one who wants lineage must want humility toward everyone (யார்க்கும் பணிவு). 125 says bowing is good for all (எல்லார்க்கும் நன்றாம் பணிதல்) and is a further wealth for the rich. Both make humility general, and each singles out the highly placed, by family or by wealth, as those it most becomes.

960 asks for humility toward all (யார்க்கும் பணிவு) from anyone who wants to keep a lineage. 963, in the next chapter, limits when bowing is called for: in abundance one must bow (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்), but in reduced circumstances one must stand high (சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). The humility of 960 is thus not meant to cover bending under want.

961 says to give up things that would diminish one (குன்ற வருப விடல்) even if they are of a kind one cannot do without (இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்). 656 gives a concrete instance: even if you must watch your mother go hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), do not do what the worthy condemn. Both state a refusal that holds against necessity, one for honour and one for clean action.

961 tells one to drop whatever lowers one's standing, however necessary. 1028 says those raising their family have no proper season, and that if they idle and stand on honour (மடிசெய்து மானம் கருத) it will be ruined; Parimelazhagar takes the thing ruined to be the family. Honour kept by declining work is here a cause of loss, which limits how far 961's 'give it up' can be taken.

Parimelazhagar reads 961's இன்றி அமையா as things without which one would not survive, so the verse puts standing above life. 131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life (உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்) because it gives excellence. The same ranking, a value kept ahead of survival, is made for honour in one chapter and for conduct in the other.

652 says to avoid any action that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை), which makes renown one of the tests of an act. 962 says those who want renown together with great manliness will not do unworthy things even for renown (சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யார்). 962 therefore narrows 652's test: bringing fame does not by itself make an act fit to do.

962 refuses unworthy acts even when they would bring renown (சீரினும்). 113 says to let go at once of gain that departs from fairness even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்). Both have the form 'even if it yields the thing you want, not by this means', applied to fame in one and to profit in the other.

963's first half says that in abundance one must bow (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்). 125 says bowing is good for all and for the rich it is a wealth of its own (செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து). Both attach humility especially to prosperity; 963 then adds the opposite duty for hard times, which 125 does not address.

963 says that in small and shrunken circumstances one must hold oneself high (சிறிய சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). 680 says those whose domain is small (உறைசிறியார்), fearing their own people's trembling, will bow to the greater and accept terms (கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). They conflict if 963's 'reduced state' includes weakness of position before a stronger party; if 963 is only about poverty and personal bearing, 680 is separate advice on statecraft.

963 asks for an upright bearing (உயர்வு) when one's means have shrunk. 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called worth (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 988 supplies the ground for 963's demand: want does not itself lower a person, so there is no reason to stoop in it.

964 says people who have come down from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை) are like hair fallen from the head. 973 says those who are not low are not low even when placed low (கீழிருந்தும் கீழல்லார் கீழல்லவர்). They conflict if 964's நிலை means outward rank or station; on Parimelazhagar's reading it means the high standard the well-born hold themselves to, so the fall is their own doing and the verses agree.

124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his position (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain. 964 uses the same word for the opposite case: those who descend from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்த) are like hair off the head. Together they give the two ends of one scale, both measured by whether a person keeps to their நிலை.

965 uses the kundri seed (குன்றி) for the smallest measure: a lowering act of that size brings down people like hills. 277 uses the same seed for its two colours: people red outside like the kundri and black within like its tip (புறங்குன்றி ... முக்கிற் கரியார்). The seed serves once as a unit of smallness and once as a figure of a fair surface with a dark spot, and in both verses the small dark thing is what counts.

965 sets a hill against a kundri seed: the hill-like sink through a lowering act the size of the seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). 433 sets a millet seed against a palmyra: those ashamed of blame treat a millet-sized fault as palm-sized. Both use a pair of extreme sizes to say that for people of standing a small fault is not small, 965 as an outcome and 433 as an attitude.

965 plays on குன்று: those like a hill (குன்றின் அனையார்) will dwindle (குன்றுவர்). 898 has the same play: if those like a hill (குன்றன்னார்) intend ruin (குன்ற மதிப்பின்), those who seemed established perish with their line. Parimelazhagar takes 898's hill-like ones to be ascetics, so the same figure marks people who can be brought low in 965 and people who bring others low in 898.

966 asks what is gained by going and standing behind those who scorn you (இகழ்வார் பின் சென்று நிலை). 1033 says only those who eat by their own ploughing truly live, and all others bow to eat and go behind (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). Both use 'going behind' another as the picture of a dependent life, and 1033 names the livelihood that avoids it.

966 says standing in the train of those who scorn you brings neither renown nor the gods' land. 1053 says that even asking has a certain beauty (ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when one stands before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று). What 966 rejects is therefore not dependence as such but dependence on people who despise the one who comes to them.

967 says that being called ruined, in that very state, is better than living by following those who do not accept you (வாழ்தலின் ... கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று). 183 says dying yields more of what virtue promises than staying alive by backbiting and falsehood (பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்). Both use the form 'than living this way, death is better', for dishonourable dependence in one and for dishonest speech in the other.

967 prefers being called ruined to a life got by following those who reject you. 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). In both, a life that cannot be lived on one's own terms, without honour or without the power to give, is ranked below death.

968 asks whether a life that tends the flesh is a medicine (மருந்தோ) once greatness has lost its dignity; Parimelazhagar takes this as a medicine against dying. 82 says that eating while the guest waits outside is not to be wanted even if the food were the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்தெனினும்). Both raise the idea of an immortality-medicine only to rank it below a duty, honour in one and hospitality in the other.

968 questions the worth of a life that merely feeds the body (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) when dignity is gone. 1017 says those governed by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் ... நாண் துறவார்). The chapters on honour and on shame reach the same ordering of life and self-respect.

969 likens the honourable to the கவரிமா that will not live once it loses its hair (மயிர் நீப்பின் வாழா). 964 likens people fallen from their position to hair that has fallen from the head (தலையின் இழிந்த மயிர்). The chapter uses hair twice: in 964 the fallen person is the worthless hair, and in 969 the loss of a hair is the loss the animal will not outlive.

969 says those like the கவரிமா give up life when their honour is at stake (உயிர் நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்). 779 asks who could reproach as failures those who die so that what they vowed is not broken (இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவார்). Dying to avoid going back on what one stands for appears as a matter of civil honour in 969 and as a soldier's vow in 779.

970 sets disgrace against radiance: the world worships the ஒளி of those who will not live when இளி comes. 971 defines the same two words: one's ஒளி is abundance of aspiration, and one's இளி is saying 'we will live without it' (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்). In both, disgrace is a way of going on living, and radiance belongs to those who refuse it.

970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of the honourable who do not live on in disgrace. 235 says that a ruin which is growth and a death which is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are hard to reach except for the skilled. 235 gives the general idea that 970 applies: a death can leave a person present in fame.

970 praises those who will not live when disgrace comes (இளிவரின் வாழாத). 240 says those who live free of blame are the ones who live, and those who live without renown are the ones who do not (இசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழாதவர்). Both deny that survival under disgrace counts as living; 970 adds that the world honours those who act on this.
